terms.means: The center names the defensive front before the snap. The book counts only five fronts: Odd, Under, Over, Even and Jam/Bear. The front word is then paired with a scheme call such as Doom or Ringo.
The linebacker the center and QB agree on as the start of the protection count. Also called the Mike point or Play point. Every sort and slide call is built from it.
Stance depth, called so the whole line sets the same. Level 1 puts the down hand even with the near tip of the ball, Level 2 even with the center's toes, Level 3 even with the center's heels.
A second call made after the first one when the defensive line stems, the linebackers slide or a safety rotates. The line keeps its eyes up for it.
Visual signals from the line to the back in pass protection. A lineman points at a defender, or taps his hip or his helmet, so the back knows who he is responsible for without words.

Calls start with the center and work outward, and every lineman echoes them. Before the snap the line also reads the open side, closed side, slot and safeties and voices what it sees with calls like Press, 9, Storm and Thru. Getting to the line early keeps the communication ahead of the cadence.
The base spacing used in the open field, about two feet between each lineman and between the tackle and tight end.
About three feet between blockers. Used to stretch the front and widen the space between defenders.
About six inches between blockers. Used in short yardage and goal line to limit penetration.
Any split rule widened or narrowed so the blocker starts where he can best do his job. The line may mix split types on a single play to improve angles and leverage.
Line of scrimmage.
Coaching point.
Point of attack, the spot the run is aimed at.
Most dangerous man, the defender who can hurt the play soonest. Many backside and sort rules are built on it.
Pre-snap look.
Angle of departure, the first-step angle out of the stance.
End man on the line of scrimmage, the widest defender on the line to a side.
The side the run is called to.
The side away from the call.
The space between two neighboring blockers. In defensive ID the gaps get letters, with plus for the strong side and minus for the weak side.
In 2/3 Jet and 200/300 Jet protection, the side the protection digit sends the line to.
In Jet protection, the side opposite the digit side, where the line sorts or slides from the center's point.
Playside guard. The book also uses PST for the playside tackle, BSG and BST for the backside guard and tackle, and OC for the center.
A defensive lineman is on the line of scrimmage head up on the blocker or on either of his shoulders.
The nearest defender over the blocker is off the line by a yard or more.
The side the Y tight end is on.
The side away from the Y tight end.
The side of the formation where a tight end is attached next to the tackle.
The side of the formation with no tight end attached to the tackle.

Each defensive lineman's alignment gets a number so the line can state it exactly: 0 is head up on the center, 2i inside shade of the guard, 2 head up on the guard, 3 outside shade of the guard, 4i inside shade of the tackle, 4 head up on the tackle, 5 outside shade of the tackle, 6i inside shade of the tight end, 6 head up on the tight end, 9 outside the tight end. Gaps get letters.

The gap letters: A is between center and guard, B between guard and tackle, C between tackle and tight end (or outside the tackle with no tight end), D outside the tight end. Plus means strong side, minus weak side.
A nose or tackle aligned on the center, either angled or tight on one shoulder.
The open space over a lineman who is uncovered.
A call that the defensive end has moved out to a 9 technique or wider.
An exchange look over the tight end: a defensive end or outside linebacker is outside the tight end and the strong safety is over him.
An exchange look over the tight end with a linebacker or end outside the tight end and a tagged linebacker over him.
Three defenders on or outside the tackle to the open or closed side, any mix of linemen, linebackers and backs. Also called Kong.
Two defenders on or outside the tackle to the open or closed side, any mix of linemen, linebackers and backs. Calls like Hog and Fan answer a Look.
A linebacker or back walked up on the line in the A gap inside a 3 technique.
A linebacker or back aligned over an uncovered guard.
A linebacker or back aligned over an uncovered center.
A defender on or near the line who is not playing coverage.
A two look where a defensive tackle is over the offensive tackle and the end is outside him on the line. Also used to name an odd-spaced defense out of 43 personnel.
The defense has a down defender on each of the playside guard, tackle and tight end.
A call by the tight end or tackle that the Sam and strong safety are both on the line in a threatening position. Storm Triple is the zone answer.
The free safety is down in the box to the weak side, inside the tight end or tackle at seven yards or less.
The strong safety is down in the box to the strong side, inside the tight end or tackle at seven yards or less.
The free safety is down on the line of scrimmage to the weak side.
The strong safety is down on the line of scrimmage to the strong side.
No defender on or over a lineman, also called a voided bubble. Also used for a linebacker missing from an odd front.
Two defenders aligned next to each other on the line.
Two defensive linemen with space between them, not side by side.
The linebackers have shifted to the strong side.
The linebackers have shifted to the weak side.
A linebacker stacked directly behind the zero technique nose.
A linebacker is the force player on the line of scrimmage. The book calls this Backer Force.
No linebacker force on the line. The book calls this Non Backer Force.
The slot defender is tight on the slot receiver. The tackles call it in 3x1 and 2x2 sets. It can bring an Alert Push to the guard and a Ringo or Lucky Out call in Jet protection.
Warns the guard that a slot defender who is topped and pressed may blitz.
The area between the ends at linebacker depth, or outside the ends on the line. A linebacker in a Hip spot counts. Any defender inside it is in the box.
A linebacker tucked just outside and behind a defensive end. He is counted as in the box.
The defense's personnel does not match the offensive grouping the usual way, for example base defense against 11 personnel or nickel against 12.
Center's front call: he is covered and both guards are uncovered.
Center's front call: he is uncovered and both guards are covered.
Center's front call: the weak guard and center are covered, the strong guard is uncovered. Also called G-Bubble.
Center's front call: the strong guard and center are covered, the weak guard is uncovered. Also called Adjacent.
Center's front call: both guards and the center are covered.
Center's front call: all three inside linemen are covered and the tight end has an exchange look over him (Choke, Dubs or Vice).

A two-digit front code. The first digit names the line: 2 Under, 5 Over, 4 Even, 3 Double Bubble. The second names the second level: 3 Sam on the line, 5 Will on, 7 Sam, Mike and Will all in the box, 9 Sam and Will both on, 4 four linebackers. So 25 is Under with the Will on, 57 is Over with all three backers in the box.
Front code 3: both guards are uncovered, so there is a bubble on each side of the center.
Added to a front name when the nose is a shade (1 technique) away from the 3 technique, as in Under G.

The center and playside guard work together on any zone run. Technique and landmarks follow the run concept (Tite, Mid or Wide). It still applies when the center is covered backside, and he must tell the backside guard. Examples in the book: 5-4 and 7-6 Wanda, 8-9 Zap.
A Single on Tite, Mid or Wide Zone against a shaded nose with the Mike inside. Chip is added to any combination whenever the designated linebacker is aligned inside; it also tags Double and Triple.
Mid or Wide Zone call when the center is uncovered: he goes through to the designated linebacker and the playside guard man-reaches his defender. Driven by the play and where the backer sits.

Mid or Wide Zone alert when the defense brings zone pressure away from the run. The surface shuts off the backside pressure and creates a cutback lane, for example a Double turning into a Single on the move.
The playside tackle and tight end work together on a zone run. The tackle makes the call, and it is required against a 6 technique.
Added to a combination when it is working up to a defensive back instead of a linebacker, for example Push Triple or Single Push. The center communicates it.
Playside tackle's call on 8-9 hole Wide Zone. The tight end stabs and slams the 5 technique to keep the D gap wide.
The combination between the Y and F tight ends on 8-9 hole Wide Zone runs.
The tight end starts a three-man combination of guard, tackle and tight end on Wide Zone, usually when the defense shows Storm pressure.
The playside guard and tackle work together on any zone run. Technique and landmarks follow the run concept. Examples in the book: 14-15 F-Sift, 18-19 Zap.
The uncovered tackle's call on 8-9 hole Wide Zone. The tackle stabs and slams the 3 technique to keep the C gap wide. Only used against a 9 technique.
Backside combination between the center and backside guard on Tite, Mid and Wide Zone. The center makes the call.
Backside combination between the covered backside guard and backside tackle on Tite, Mid and Wide Zone. The guard makes the call.

Backside combination between the covered backside tackle and tight end for the end and middle linebacker on Tite, Mid and Wide Zone. The tackle makes the call. It can work up to a safety, linebacker or most dangerous man.
Backside combination between the covered tight end and the wing tight end for the end and the outside backer or safety.
Backside combination between the two wing tight ends for the outside backer and the force player, on zone runs from 13 personnel.
Backside call for center, backside guard, backside tackle and tight end against a Jam or Bear front on Wide and Mid Zone. It also ties the playside guard into the scheme.
A five or six man call on Wide Zone that puts the whole surface, linemen and tight end, on tracks. Used to pick up pressures like Pirate, 25 Smack and 25 Wham cross dog.
A three man call for center, playside guard and playside tackle on open side zone runs when movement such as Pirate is expected.

Backside call for center, backside guard and backside tackle against Under, Jam and Bear fronts and against a Zero Stack, on Wide and Mid Zone. The center calls it. The backside guard uses Wide A footwork and has no help.
The Tite Zone version of Gang: center, backside guard and backside tackle against Under, Jam and Bear fronts. The backside guard starts with Tite B technique, reads the linebacker and reacts.
A lineman or tight end announces he will block the man aligned over him on the line. Used playside or backside, in the run game or pass protection.
A playside lineman's single block at the point of attack. Tite Zone (4-5), Mid Zone (7-6) and Wide Zone (8-9) each have their own reach technique and landmarks.
The backside tackle's technique on zone runs: he works through the line and blocks the most dangerous man from the first level to the second.
The backside tackle sifts from the line to the second or third level, owning his playside gap. He protects against a linebacker running through first.
The backside tight end's version of the sift, working from the line up to the second or third level.
Playside tackle and guard call on Tite Zone when the playside backer is stacked or inside the 3 technique. There must be a 9 technique playside.
Center and playside guard call on Tite Zone against a shaded nose.
A playside lineman's block at the point of attack on perimeter and transportation series runs.
A quick pass set on draw plays that invites the end to rush upfield.
A playside lineman blocks down on a defender in the gap inside him.
A covered playside lineman drives his man straight back for vertical displacement. Used on 4-5 hole Tite Zone and 2-3 hole gap runs.
Playside tackle's call on gap runs against a Look. He uses Base Drive technique, the call tells the line there is a Look on the open side, and he may collect the end.
Guard tells the tackle to block the widest defender in a Look, playside or backside. If the defense folds, the alert is Area.
Turn Out. The tight end tells the tackle to block out on the defender over the tight end.
The backside tackle or tight end drives a down defender to cut off his pursuit. Used on 4-5 hole Tite Zone.
Center and playside guard double the nose up to the Will (or Jack). Against a two-gapping nose the alert is Feed Ace.
A technique tag added to a double team against a two-gapping defender: Feed Ace, Feed Doom, Feed Tram.
The center blocks back on an A gap defender.
Center's call: the playside guard blocks down on the nose and the center chokes back.
Playside tackle and guard double the tackle vertically up to the Mike. Against a two-gapping tackle the alert is Feed Doom. Example: 12-13 Duo.
Playside tackle and guard double the tackle up to the Will on gap schemes. Both keep inside head position.
The playside tackle works with the tight end for the point, the Mike. Feed Tram against a two-gapper. Example: 12-13 Duo.
Playside tackle and tight end double the end up to the Will or Jack.
The playside tackle starts inside with gap footwork alongside the guard, then converts to a Tram with the tight end if the 2i does not loop. Example: 12-13 Duo.
Against Jam and Bear fronts the playside tackle, guard and center all stay inside-gap conscious. Example: 12-13 Duo.
An all-down scheme on gap-trap runs: playside tackle and guard block down to their inside gap and the center chokes back. The center calls it against Bear fronts. Deuce can convert to Dallas.
Backside call: center and backside guard double the tackle up to the Will. Rake is to the right, Lawn to the left. The center calls it. Example: 12-13 Duo.
The left-hand version of Rake: center and backside guard double the tackle to the Will.
Backside tackle or tight end technique: block the most dangerous man from the inside B gap out to the C gap. Example: 12-13 Punch.
Backside tackle and guard technique when covered on the outside gap. Example: 12-13 Duo.
On trap plays the playside guard tells the tackle that the guard will take the designated linebacker. Example: 30-31 Trap. A dummy Doom or Ringo/Lucky may be added.
On trap plays the playside guard tells the tackle that the tackle now has the designated linebacker. Example: 30-31 Trap.
A fake call such as Doom or Ringo/Lucky made on a trap to disguise the real scheme.

Backside call: the tackle blocks the Will while the guard blocks out on the end. On page 22 the center makes it after checking the Will's alignment, for draw runs or the backside of Duo. On page 46 the guard makes it.
Playside tackle's call on 13-12 Charlie or Barkley when there is no B gap defender to Deuce. It tells the backside guard he now pulls for the first defender off the ball (Oh Pull). Game plan only.
Playside tight end and wing combination: block the end up to the playside linebacker, or track to that linebacker.
Tag in the play description for jet motion away from the point of attack on a run, play action or screen.
Tag in the play description for jet motion toward the point of attack on a run, play action or screen.
Tag that pulls the run's targeting back one spot against single-high and tells the surface to block the defense as spots.
Tag that pushes the run's targeting up one spot against single-high and tells the surface to block the defense as spots.

The center's three or four man sort that starts a sort-slide scheme in 2/3 Jet and 200/300 Jet. He splits the formation down the middle and points to the first linebacker inside-out away from the call; MDM rules run from that point. The tackle to the call side is locked on the contain end. The back scans. Ringo and Lucky are the right and left versions.
The opposite-side version of Ringo. Same sort-slide mechanics with the center's point set away from the call.
In Ringo or Lucky, the tackle to the call side is locked on the contain end and is not part of the sort.
The back checks for blitz from the inside out before releasing. He works against five-man pressure and is the catch against four-man pressure.
A defender counted as certain to rush, usually a down lineman. Non-known rushers are backers and backs who may or may not come, and the sort and the back's scan are built around them.
A sub-front rusher who moves or stands up. Ringo and Lucky can treat him as a known rusher: the line declares him down (Down Down) and tracks him. Game plan specific.
Ringo or Lucky Stack warns the sort-side guard and tackle that the point defender can blitz away from the sort side. If he does, they get no center help and are effectively Stick.

The QB flips a Ringo to a Lucky or a Lucky to a Ringo when two non-known rushers sit to the protecting back's side, or against a Bug or Tuff backer in a six-man box, so the back can release. A Middle Flipper is also possible.

Ringo or Lucky Out moves the point to the second non-known rusher past the middle of the formation. The sort then runs outside-in from that player. Used by structure and game plan, including against a Press slot.
Added to a sort call, as in Ringo Tuff or Rip Tuff, when a backer or back is walked up in the A or B gap. Also used against an Abby front with man coverage.

A two man guard and tackle sort on each side, started by the center against odd spacing, 34 personnel and guard-bubble fronts in base. The center taps his helmet, and each guard and tackle points to the man they sort first, inside-out or outside-in by personnel. Used in 200/300 and 2/3 Jet.
The center taps his helmet to start a Sort-Sort or Drag-Drag, and the guard and tackle answer by pointing.
Inside-out: the guard sorts the inside threat and the tackle the outside one. The normal order of a Sort against most odd looks.
Outside-in: the guard and tackle sort from the outside threat in. Used when the odd front shows Up looks or a Saw pressure threat, when two of the same type stack to a side, and by game plan.
When two defenders of the same type are stacked to a side, the sort goes outside-in. The page also labels this the Mug rule.

A one-side outside-in guard and tackle sort shown against odd fronts with a nickel or a mugged backer, called with a side (Ollie Rt) and paired with a Sort or Giant to the other side. The page shows it in diagrams only and gives no prose definition.
A three-man slide to one side, shown opposite an Ollie and paired with the Good call. The book labels it in diagrams but does not define it in prose.

A four man sort by the QB (or center) that starts a gap scheme: the center borrows the backside guard so the protection can turn, and points to the first linebacker inside-out toward the call. Used against three-down fronts and to trump Sort-Sort, leaving one rusher for the back. The line pushes to the widest threat unless it is a five-man overload. Roger and Louie are the right and left versions.
The opposite-side version of Roger, the four man gap sort.

First Name. A three man slide sort by the QB against an Abby front that sends the slide to the fourth element. The back gets the A gap away from the call and no longer scans. Wade and Phillips are the right and left versions.
Last Name. The opposite-side version of Wade.

Good Rt or Good Lt answers a Jam front with seven threats that is trying to force a minus call and a hot throw. Good goes to the bigger end man on the line, or the better of two like bodies, and the back gets the smaller one. The back checks the backer in his A gap to the widest rusher on the scat side and cheats up only if backers are walked up. Pairs with Giant to the call and Drag Dual away.

The Timely protection version of Ringo against four-down fronts: a three-for-three man call where the center points to the first linebacker inside-out away from the call and man rules run from the point. Same alerts: back scans, Flipper, Stick on the nose, a mugged backer over the center belongs to the back, minus call possible. Ram and Lion are the right and left versions.
The opposite-side version of Ram.

A three or four man slide sort by the center in 200/300 Scat and Scram. He points to the first linebacker inside-out toward the call, usually the Mike, and MDM rules run past the point. The playside tackle sorts every pressure inside-out because there is no scanning back. The QB can override the point. Rip and Liz are the right and left versions.
The opposite-side version of Rip.

A five man sort by the QB in 200/300 Scat and Scram: the line slides toward the call to handle an overload. The tackle away from the call sticks on the 3 technique, may Big Dual a guard bubble, and bangs back outside if the 3 technique drops. Ralph and Lester are the right and left versions.
The opposite-side version of Ralph.

A one or two man sort by the backside guard and tackle in 200/300 Scat and Scram. Both block most-dangerous-man inside-out and stay in constant verbal and visual contact. Alert for a Squeeze on the move.

An on-the-move adjustment inside Big Dual or Drag-Drag where the backside pair tighten down to inside threats. Not allowed with a minus call. The book names it in alerts and diagrams but does not define it in prose.

A two man guard and tackle sort on each side for 2/3 Scat and Scram against Odd and Jam spacing. The center calls it with a helmet tap and both sides drag inside-out. Alert Big Dual and Squeeze against Jam, Bear and Cub fronts.
Diagram label for a rusher the count leaves unblocked, who becomes the QB's hot throw. No Hot means every rusher is accounted for.

A five man full slide by the QB in 58 and 59 toward the call, to handle overloads. Each lineman owns the gap toward the turn, the turn tackle no longer handles a 3 technique loop, and the back protects to the call. Alerts: Push Thru for extra inside threats, plus or minus in 58/59 and 358/359, and a QB line call against zero pressure in Scat and Jet.
Alert in the R/L slide that an additional inside threat must be passed through the slide.
A tackle or guard locked on his man in a given protection. An alert call may adjust it.
The '-' call: the five linemen block the five known rushers on the line. Used against Jam, Bear and Cub fronts. Code words Poker and Bullseye hide it. No Squeeze or Hard calls go with it.
A code word for the minus call.
A code word for the minus call.

A three man area call by the center: he sets for the Mike over him, and the guards and tackles area off any crossing backers and ends. The center flashes the minus signal to the backs. Usable by QB or line in 200/300 and 2/3 Jet.
Six blockers on the five known rushers plus the tight end turning out on the choke player. Used against Bear and Cub fronts, mostly in play pass. No Squeeze or Hard with it. A code word can hide it.

Blow R or L: a three or four man slide of center, guard and tackle with gap responsibilities. The center can borrow the backside guard, calls Stay to keep the guard in his gap against dogs and stunts, and Ringo or Lucky can convert to Blow on the move.
Center's reminder inside a Blow slide that the guard holds his gap against dogs and stunts.

Solid R or L: a three man area call by an uncovered guard that he is setting for the backer over him. It is a help call; if the backer does not dog, the guard becomes the inside sideboard for the tackle.

A covered guard and the protecting back swap when the back's man is Tuff in the A gap: the guard takes the back's man and the back takes the 3 technique. The guard hip-taps the back. It can be sight-adjusted on the move. Applies in 200/300 and 2/3 Jet, never from the gun.
The QB moves from under center to shotgun to remove any Hard calls, and tells the line with Gun-Gun.
Tells the next man on the line to go past the man he has in protection, or tells the outside player he needs no help and can fall back inside.
Made by the outside player on the stick side on a line game: it warns the inside lineman that the down lineman is spiking inside.
Center tells both guards he is going away from the original slide side. The backside guard now has help and the playside guard loses his.

A covered guard and uncovered tackle tie to a targeted backer in a B combination. If he does not blitz, the tackle is the inside sideboard for the tight end. The call keeps guard and tackle connected.
A two man area call by the uncovered guard to the tackle that they block the Look. Playside or backside of the protection.
Tackle and tight end, both covered, each block the man over him in play pass protection.
Buddy Rt or Lt: against a three man rush in odd spacing in two-minute or long yardage, three double teams on the line. Called when the backers are deep.
A backside exchange: the tight end blocks out and the wing wraps around, or the backside tackle blocks out and the tight end wraps around.
Backside exchange: the guard blocks out on the lineman and the tackle pulls around for the inside backer.
Backside call: the guard takes the Buck backer and the tackle fans to the Will. It adjusts Club against a 34 defense.
Playside call by the tackle: the guard pulls for the Sam while the tackle blocks down. The tight end must be ready to add a call.
Playside call by the tackle for an exchange with the tight end: the tight end blocks down on the end and the tackle pulls for the outside backer.
The center pulls on a cross scheme.
The guard pulls around for the Mike, mirroring up into the first open hole.
Playside call by the tight end against a 9 technique: guard and tight end exchange the Sam and the end.
The playside guard pulls flat and blocks the end man on the line.
Playside call: the guard blocks down on the nose and the center pulls for the Mike.
Playside call by the tackle: the tight end releases to the second level for the Sam and the tackle draw-sets the end. Be ready for a Plug call with it.
Exchange between center and backside guard: the center blocks back and the guard pulls for the designated backer. The center makes every Fred call.
Blocking a zone instead of a man. Used as an alert in Fan when the defense folds, and in the Middle, Solid and Fan area calls.
